cues.text: A Fallen Particle
On Easter Sunday, March 31, 1331, the first Mass of the day was celebrated in the small village of Blanot in Burgundy.
The parish vicar, Hugues de la Baume , was distributing Communion when a small particle of the Host fell unnoticed from the mouth of a widow named Jacquette.
It landed on the linen cloth the altar servers held beneath the hands of each communicant.
"The Body of Our Lord Fell"
An altar server assisting at the Mass, Thomas Caillot, caught what the priest had not.
He called the priest back to the rail, saying: "Father, you must return to the rail because the Body of Our Lord fell from the mouth of this lady onto the cloth."
The priest returned, finding a small, distinct stain of blood soaked into the linen, replacing the fallen particle.
A Stain That Would Not Wash Out
The priest repeatedly attempted to wash the stain from the cloth, but each attempt only left the mark darker and larger.
The water in his basin itself turned bloody; unable to remove it by any means, he cut the stained square from the larger cloth.
Before the assembled congregation, he declared, in words later recorded, that this was the Precious Blood of Christ.
An Investigation and Two Papal Confirmations
The Bishop of Autun, Pierre Bertrand , opened a formal inquiry into the events soon afterward.
He interviewed the witnesses present at the Mass, and sent the resulting documentation to Pope John XXII.
The pope confirmed the sign as a genuine Eucharistic miracle.
Legacy
The stained cloth was hidden by nuns and parishioners through the upheavals of the French Revolution .
It was returned to the church once the danger had passed.
An eighteenth-century examination by the Bishop of Autun found the blood still bright red and the cloth itself undecayed after hundreds of years.

It remains today in a crystal reliquary at the parish church of Blanot, still solemnly exposed each year on the feast of Corpus Christi, nearly seven centuries after one small, unnoticed fall from a widow's mouth.
